In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] theory of [[conformal mapping]]s, the '''area theorem'''
gives an [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] satisfied by
the [[power series]] [[coefficient]]s of certain conformal mappings.
The theorem is called by that name, not because of its implications, but rather because the proof uses
the notion of [[area]].

==Statement==
Suppose that <math>f</math> is [[analytic function|analytic]] and [[injective function|injective]] in the punctured
[[open set|open]] [[unit disk]]
<math>\mathbb D\setminus\{0\}</math> and has the power series representation
:<math>
f(z)= \frac 1z + \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n,\qquad z\in \mathbb D\setminus\{0\},
</math>
then the coefficients <math>a_n</math> satisfy
:<math>
\sum_{n=0}^\infty n|a_n|^2\le 1.
</math>

==Proof==
The idea of the proof is to look at the area uncovered by the image of <math>f</math>.
Define for <math>r\in(0,1)</math>
:<math>\gamma_r(\theta):=f(r\,e^{-i\theta}),\qquad \theta\in[0,2\pi].
</math>
Then <math>\gamma_r</math> is a simple closed curve in the plane.
Let <math>D_r</math> denote the unique bounded connected component of
<math>\mathbb C\setminus\gamma_r([0,2\pi])</math>. The existence and
uniqueness of <math>D_r</math> follows from [[Jordan curve theorem|Jordan's curve theorem]].

If <math>D</math> is a domain in the plane whose boundary
is a [[Smooth function#Smoothness|smooth]] simple closed curve <math>\gamma</math>,
then
:<math>
\mathrm{area}(D)=\int_\gamma x\,dy=-\int_\gamma y\,dx\,,
</math>
provided that <math>\gamma</math> is positively [[orientation (topology)|oriented]]
around <math>D</math>.
This follows easily, for example, from [[Green's theorem]].
As we will soon see, <math>\gamma_r</math> is positively oriented around
<math>D_r</math> (and that is the reason for the minus sign in the
definition of <math>\gamma_r</math>). After applying the [[chain rule]]
and the formula for <math>\gamma_r</math>, the above expressions for
the area give
:<math>
\mathrm{area}(D_r)= \int_0^{2\pi} \Re\bigl(f(r e^{-i\theta})\bigr)\,\Im\bigl(-i\,r\,e^{-i\theta}\,f'(r e^{-i\theta})\bigr)\,d\theta = -\int_0^{2\pi} \Im\bigl(f(r e^{-i\theta})\bigr)\,\Re\bigl(-i\,r\,e^{-i\theta}\,f'(r e^{-i\theta})\bigr)d\theta.
</math>
Therefore, the area of <math>D_r</math> also equals to the average of the two expressions on the right
hand side. After simplification, this yields
:<math>
\mathrm{area}(D_r) = -\frac 12\, \Re\int_0^{2\pi}f(r\,e^{-i\theta})\,\overline{r\,e^{-i\theta}\,f'(r\,e^{-i\theta})}\,d\theta,
</math>
where <math>\overline z</math> denotes [[complex conjugation]]. We set <math>a_{-1}=1</math> and use the power series
expansion for <math>f</math>, to get
:<math>
\mathrm{area}(D_r) = -\frac 12\, \Re\int_0^{2\pi} \sum_{n=-1}^\infty
\sum_{m=-1}^\infty
m\,r^{n+m}\,a_n\,\overline{a_m}\,e^{i\,(m-n)\,\theta}\,d\theta\,.
</math>
(Since <math>\int_0^{2\pi} \sum_{n=-1}^\infty\sum_{m=-1}^\infty m\,r^{n+m}\,|a_n|\,|a_m|\,d\theta<\infty\,,
</math> the rearrangement of the terms is justified.)
Now note that <math>\int_0^{2\pi} e^{i\,(m-n)\,\theta}\,d\theta</math> is <math>2\pi</math> if <math>n= m</math>
and is zero otherwise. Therefore, we get
:<math>
\mathrm{area}(D_r)= -\pi\sum_{n=-1}^\infty n\,r^{2n}\,|a_n|^2.
</math>
The area of <math>D_r</math> is clearly positive. Therefore, the right hand side
is positive. Since <math>a_{-1}=1</math>, by letting <math>r\to1</math>, the
theorem now follows.

It only remains to justify the claim that <math>\gamma_r</math> is positively oriented
around <math>D_r</math>. Let <math>r'</math> satisfy <math>r<r'<1</math>, and set
<math>z_0=f(r')</math>, say. For very small <math>s>0</math>, we may write the
expression for the [[winding number]] of <math>\gamma_s</math> around <math>z_0</math>,
and verify that it is equal to <math>1</math>. Since, <math>\gamma_t</math> does
not pass through <math>z_0</math> when <math>t\ne r'</math>
(as <math>f</math> is injective), the invariance
of the winding number under homotopy in the complement of <math>z_0</math>
implies that the winding number of
<math>\gamma_r</math> around <math>z_0</math> is also <math>1</math>.
This implies that <math>z_0\in D_r</math> and that <math>\gamma_r</math>
is positively oriented around <math>D_r</math>, as required.

==Uses==
The inequalities satisfied by power series coefficients of conformal
mappings were of considerable interest to mathematicians prior to
the solution of the [[Bieberbach conjecture]]. The area theorem
is a central tool in this context. Moreover, the area theorem is often
used in order to prove the [[Koebe 1/4 theorem]], which is very
useful in the study of the geometry of conformal mappings.
